articles.title: Four touchdowns, no speed limit
articles.dek: Accel BeckhmJr turned seven catches into 259 yards and four scores. Mossdeep answered an early deficit with 38 of the final 45 points, beating Vermilion 45–21 to reach 10–0.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: Vermilion had just made this a game again. Chandelure had found Victreebel for a twelve-yard touchdown on third-and-eleven, the extra point had cut Mossdeep's lead to ten, and there was still a quarter plus change to play. Then Dram Marino threw deep right to Accel BeckhmJr. Sixty-six yards later, the Volts needed another answer. They would spend the rest of the afternoon looking for one.

That was BeckhmJr's third touchdown. His fourth went sixty-nine yards early in the fourth quarter. His second had gone sixty. Add the thirteen-yard opening score and you have an afternoon that left an awful lot of defenders turning toward their own end zone: seven catches, 259 yards, four touchdowns and a 45–21 Mossdeep victory. The Eclipse are 10–0. Their lead receiver has crossed a thousand yards with seven regular-season games still to play.

I don't want the final margin to erase the problem Mossdeep had to solve. Lt. Surge's Volts led 14–7 in the second quarter. They put together touchdown drives of sixty-nine and eighty yards, and Chandelure finished with three scoring throws and no interceptions. Vermilion made Michael Dorrill's defense work. The response was a passing explosion, five sacks and a stretch in which the Eclipse scored thirty-eight points to the Volts' seven.

body.speaker: Accel BeckhmJr
body.text: The short one counted too. I'd hate for everybody to get spoiled and start asking why I only went thirteen yards. Dram put the ball where I could do something with it. I tried to be considerate and save us a few extra plays.
A lead, a deficit, then the right side

Mossdeep's first opportunity came quickly. Vermilion's opening possession ended on downs after four plays and nine yards. The Eclipse needed only three plays to cover twenty-seven yards, finishing with Marino's short-right throw to BeckhmJr at 4:48 of the opening quarter. Adam Vinathorn made the extra point. A short field, a quick touchdown and an unbeaten visitor: the outline looked familiar. Vermilion refused to follow it.

The Volts answered with a nine-play, sixty-nine-yard possession. Chandelure's seventeen-yard short-left touchdown to Whiscash tied the game, then Vermilion forced Mossdeep's only punt. The next home possession lasted twelve plays and covered eighty yards. Joey Sporeter's six-yard sack did not end it. Chandelure eventually found the No. 30 Ariados on third-and-three for the three-yard touchdown, and Vermilion led with 3:40 left before halftime.

That matters when assessing the Eclipse defense. A sack inside a scoring drive is a contribution, not a stop. Mossdeep needed to finish possessions, and in this early stretch it wasn't doing so. Chandelure had a legitimate passing rhythm. Whiscash and Ariados had supplied the touchdowns, while Victreebel would finish with five catches for ninety-seven yards and Galvantula four for sixty-five. Vermilion had more than one way to move the ball.

Mossdeep's answer covered eighty-one yards in six plays. The decisive throw came on first-and-ten at 2:19: deep right to BeckhmJr, sixty yards, touchdown. There was no need to describe the entire offense as repaired on the strength of one play. There was every reason to keep testing the same part of the field. The Volts had just learned that one completion could remove a lead they had spent two lengthy possessions building.

body.speaker: Dram Marino
body.text: You still have to make the read and deliver it. A long completion doesn't give you permission to stop checking the next one. Accel made a lot out of those opportunities, and the protection gave us time to take them.

The defense then did the work I had been waiting for. Armaldo Pace sacked Chandelure for eight yards on Vermilion's next series, which ended in a punt. Mossdeep went forty-six yards in six plays, with Ninjaskamara finishing an eight-yard run up the middle on third-and-two. That was the go-ahead touchdown. Sporeter then opened the next Volts possession with a seven-yard sack, another punt followed, and Vinathorn's forty-six-yard field goal made it 24–14 before the break.

The final two minutes changed the terms of the game. Mossdeep had turned a tied score into a ten-point advantage without needing Vermilion to throw an interception or lose a fumble. Pressure shortened the home possessions, the offense took advantage of the returns to the field, and the kicker completed the last assignment. That's a sequence a defense can help create again. Waiting for the opponent to hand over the ball would have been a much less satisfying plan.
The answer lasted one snap

Dorrill's offense opened the second half with its longest touchdown possession by play count: eleven snaps and seventy-seven yards. Ninjaskamara scored from seven yards out on a run right with 3:29 left in the third. He finished with ninety-one yards and two touchdowns on thirteen carries. Poury Holt added thirteen yards on four attempts. For all the attention BeckhmJr earned, Mossdeep could still ask its ground game to complete a sustained drive.

Vermilion's next response was good football. The Volts went eighty-two yards in seven plays, surviving Shawn Mareman's five-yard sack before Chandelure hit Victreebel on third-and-eleven for the twelve-yard score. That cut the deficit to 31–21. A defense can give an opponent a difficult down and still lose the down. Mossdeep has now seen that happen against this passing attack; nobody needs to turn a comfortable final score into permission to ignore it.

Then came the one-play reply. At 1:19, Marino went deep right to BeckhmJr for sixty-six yards. Vinathorn's kick restored the seventeen-point cushion. Vermilion had spent a seven-play drive reopening the contest, and Mossdeep had spent one play closing most of that opening. It was the clearest illustration of the afternoon's imbalance: the Volts could move the ball, but they could not make the Eclipse pay enough time or attempts for their own scores.

Marino did give Vermilion another chance. Drakloak intercepted a deep-right attempt with twenty-six seconds left in the third and returned it nineteen yards. The Volts still went nowhere useful. Reggie Bite sacked Chandelure for eight yards, and that possession ended in another punt. The interception did not become a rescue because Mossdeep's defense finally treated the ensuing series as a job to finish.

On the next Eclipse possession, BeckhmJr supplied the last touchdown. Marino's deep-right completion went sixty-nine yards at 5:26 of the fourth. Four scoring catches, three of them at least sixty yards, all to the same receiver. I can admire the timing and execution while also wondering how many times the Volts needed to see the route of travel on the scoreboard. By the fourth touchdown, surprise was no longer a useful explanation.

body.speaker: Michael Dorrill
body.text: We had to answer their early drives, and we did. I liked that the defense got the ball back after the interception. The explosive plays get the attention, but that response kept us in control.
What travels to Rustboro

Marino finished sixteen of twenty-seven for 354 yards, four touchdowns and one interception. Gronkaludon contributed six catches for seventy yards, keeping the passing production from becoming entirely a one-player operation. Ninjulio Jones caught two for eighteen and Lorenzo Steel one for seven. Mossdeep's 459 total yards came on forty-six plays, compared with Vermilion's 296 on forty-nine. The Eclipse did not need to win the play-count contest to win the yardage contest emphatically.

Sporeter recorded two sacks and five pressures; Mareman added a sack and five pressures. Pace and Bite supplied the other sacks. Chandelure was dropped five times for thirty-four yards, while Marino's lone sack came with forty seconds left. The difference in protection helped decide which offense could keep producing explosive answers. Chandelure's seventeen completions on twenty-four attempts deserve acknowledgment, but the possessions ending behind the sticks cost the Volts opportunities they could not replace.

Mossdeep remains without Marshall Flock, who has four weeks left on his injury listing. This game produced no new injury entry in the recorded report, and BeckhmJr's earlier minor issue is absent from the current report. George Kipple's evolution into Marshtomp is another piece of the week's news. None of that turns the secondary into a finished product. Vermilion scored three passing touchdowns. Rustboro gets to study those, too.

The Volts are 6–4 after consecutive losses and travel to Viridian next. Their conference position remains useful; their recent results are less comforting. Mossdeep visits the 6–4 Rustboro Stone with 428 points scored and ninety-seven allowed. The Eclipse have won all five road games so far. The next opponent has a full week to think about how to stop the latest road performance from becoming a rerun.

For BeckhmJr, the immediate accounting is simpler: 1,035 receiving yards for the season, 259 of them earned here. The opening touchdown required thirteen. The last three required a defense to keep a receiver in front of it. Sixty, sixty-six, sixty-nine. Vermilion never found the answer.

art.alt: Accel BeckhmJr runs into open field in Mossdeep magenta and gold.

articles.title: One point, one stop, one escape
articles.dek: FLOAT SZN ran for 146 yards and two touchdowns, Marowak broke up Blackthorn’s tying try with a sack, and Sunyshore survived 21–20 despite Hatterene’s 368-yard afternoon.
articles.author: tessa-wren

body.text: The ball could move almost anywhere for Blackthorn except the last few yards it needed. Hatterene threw for 368 yards and three touchdowns. Sawsbuck gained 142 through the air, Exploud caught ten passes, and the Dragons reached twenty points with 2:22 left. Two points would have tied the game. Marowak reached Hatterene first, and Sunyshore's 21–20 lead survived the conversion attempt and one more Blackthorn possession.

That is the finish. The beginning belonged to a different kind of mistake: FLOAT SZN fumbled on the game's first play. The Sunyshore back spent the rest of the afternoon giving his defense something worth protecting, running for 146 yards and two touchdowns on twelve carries. His seventy-yard score on third-and-one late in the first half was the largest gain in a game full of useful Blackthorn passing plays. It was also the reason the Starseekers went to halftime ahead.

Both clubs leave Week 11 at 8–2. Karson Jones' Starseekers have won three straight and remain second in the Hoenn–Sinnoh seeding order. Clair's Dragons remain second in Kanto–Johto, but a home loss now leads directly into a visit to unbeaten Mt. Silver. Sunyshore's own next stop is Eterna. Neither side gets to turn a close game into an extended recovery period.

body.speaker: FLOAT SZN
body.text: The defense helped me after the fumble. I owed them a better next carry, and the guys blocking kept giving me chances to get there. The long run was a lot of people doing their part before I got to enjoy it.
The defense paid the first bill

FLOAT SZN's opening run went left for eight yards before the ball came loose and Blastoise recovered for Blackthorn. The Dragons had a gift and no points to show for it. Their four-play possession ended on downs after seven yards. Sunyshore's offense then punted, giving Blackthorn another chance, and the home team again turned the ball over on downs, this time after a nine-play, sixty-one-yard drive. Those empty possessions belong in any explanation of the final one-point difference.

The second stop was particularly expensive for the Dragons because it consumed real offensive production. Moving sixty-one yards is supposed to change something. Here, it changed field position without changing the scoreboard. Blackthorn would finish with sixteen first downs to Sunyshore's eleven and 385 total yards to 341. Those advantages tell us the Dragons could create opportunities. They do not tell us that every opportunity was completed.

Sunyshore took over and assembled an eleven-play, eighty-eight-yard touchdown drive. FLOAT SZN finished it with a one-yard run up the middle at 4:32 of the second quarter. Duo SON 😭 made the extra point, and the Starseekers finally led 7–0. The possession offered a useful counterweight to the later seventy-yard dash: Jones' offense also moved the ball over a long series and completed the short-yardage work at the end.

Blackthorn answered in seven plays. Hatterene's deep-right throw to Octillery went seventeen yards for a touchdown with 2:44 left in the half. The extra point tied the score. Sunyshore punted on its next series, but consecutive sacks by Zack Bear and Fred Whirler pushed Hatterene backward on the following Blackthorn possession. The Dragons punted. Each offense had reached seven, and each defense had shown it could interrupt a possession before the other side found the finish.

The next exchange of punts left Sunyshore with very little time before halftime. On third-and-one at 0:37, FLOAT SZN ran up the middle for seventy yards and a touchdown. The situation called for a yard; the result gave Jones seven points after the conversion. Blackthorn's earlier long drives had required a series of successful decisions. This one required one successful run at exactly the wrong moment for the home team.

body.speaker: DeZhaun Watzon
body.text: Sometimes you spend a drive knocking on doors and the running back finds the whole hallway open. I was very happy to let him give the tour. We needed that one before the half.
A two-touchdown cushion gets very small

Blackthorn opened the second half with another substantial possession that ended on downs: nine plays and sixty-four yards. Sunyshore then drove eighty-eight yards in ten plays. DeZhaun Watzon hit Jolt Vick with a three-yard short-right touchdown pass at 1:07 of the third, and the extra point made it 21–7. The Starseekers had three touchdown drives, two of them eighty-eight yards long and the other accelerated by FLOAT SZN's breakaway.

The Dragons had little trouble making the fourth quarter interesting. Their next touchdown came on fourth-and-three, Hatterene finding Tinkaton short left for four yards at 5:18. This time the late-down throw crossed the necessary line and reached the end zone. Cacturne's kick reduced the deficit to seven. A Sunyshore punt followed, with Vigoroth's four-yard sack on third-and-five helping force it. The two-touchdown cushion had survived less than a full quarter.

Blackthorn's next drive covered ninety-one yards in six plays. Hatterene finished it with a thirteen-yard deep-left touchdown to Sawsbuck at 2:22. Sawsbuck's six catches produced 142 yards, including a forty-four-yard gain elsewhere in the game. He gave the Dragons the kind of downfield production that can overturn a deficit quickly. The problem was now very specific: Blackthorn had twenty points, Sunyshore twenty-one, and the conversion would determine whether the next possession began level.

Clair went for two. At 2:20, Marowak sacked Hatterene for a three-yard loss on the try. The score stayed 21–20. It was a separate conversion play, which is why its importance exceeds what a glance at the ordinary sack totals conveys. Sunyshore had two sacks in the regular defensive statistics. The stop that prevented the tying points came on a snap with a different immediate purpose and an enormous effect on the finish.

body.speaker: Marowak
body.text: Everybody had to keep their job on that play. I got there, but I didn't do the whole thing myself. We still knew they'd get another chance if we couldn't finish with the ball.

They did get another chance. Sunyshore's next possession ended with a punt at 1:52. The Dragons began their final drive at 1:43 and immediately gained eleven yards on Hatterene's short-right pass to Exploud. Then Furret lost a yard, two passes fell incomplete, and the game came down to fourth-and-eleven. Hatterene completed a short-left pass to Seadra for nine yards. Serp Gardener made the tackle. Nine was useful everywhere except this down.

Watzon knelt twice, and the Starseekers escaped. Blackthorn had scored thirteen unanswered fourth-quarter points, gained more total yards, made more first downs and won the turnover count. It still needed two more yards on the final completion. That is why I resist treating a close final score as either proof of an undeserving winner or a complete account of the game. Sunyshore allowed a lot of progress and repeatedly defended the exact place where progress had to become points.
The matchup behind the margin

The rushing difference was severe: Sunyshore gained 166 yards on twenty carries, Blackthorn seventeen on thirteen. FLOAT SZN supplied most of the first total, while the Dragons' longest listed rush was Furret's ten-yarder. Hatterene had to carry a far larger share of the offense, attempting forty-two passes to Watzon's twenty-two. Both quarterbacks avoided interceptions. The Starseekers' advantage came from getting enough points without asking their passer to match Hatterene's volume.

Watzon finished thirteen of twenty-two for 175 yards and the touchdown to Jolt Vick. Scol Alexander led Sunyshore's receivers with sixty-one yards on three catches; Fera LaGatr added forty-five, Vick forty and MF STOMP twenty-nine. Those numbers won't win a comparison with Blackthorn's receiving totals. They did give Sunyshore enough passing help to complement the run game, including the short scoring throw that established the fourteen-point lead.

Exploud's ten catches on eleven targets gave Hatterene a dependable outlet, while Sawsbuck provided the larger gains. Ninjask caught five passes for eighty-nine yards but is now listed out two weeks. Grovyle remains out five. The timing of Ninjask's injury is not established in the game record, so the sensible conclusion is about availability going forward: Clair has fewer receiving options for Mt. Silver than the final Blackthorn passing line might suggest.

Sunyshore still has Myles Gabite listed out two weeks. FLOAT SZN's response helps Jones manage that absence, but the opening fumble and the difficulty closing the game with possession are worth carrying into the Eterna preparation. Five punts left the defense repeatedly responsible for protecting a slim advantage. A seventy-yard touchdown is a wonderful solution when it happens; it is a difficult weekly requirement to set for any running back.

For Blackthorn, the next opponent makes completion of drives urgent. Mt. Silver has allowed sixty-eight points in ten games and just shut out Eterna. For Sunyshore, the Thorns offer a chance to build on an important road win against a division leader. The Starseekers will arrive with a three-game winning streak and a finish their defense can name precisely: Marowak on the try, Serp Gardener on fourth down, and one point still standing.

art.alt: Sunyshore’s Marowak reaches Blackthorn quarterback Hatterene on the decisive two-point try.

articles.title: Five for Skattebo, nothing for Fortree
articles.dek: Dam Skattebo scored five rushing touchdowns and Medicham recorded five sacks as Saffron answered its Mossdeep defeat with a 52–0 demolition of the Skyhawks.
articles.author: rowan-vale

body.text: Dam Skattebo scored five times. Medicham sacked the quarterback five times. Fortree's scoring contribution was zero, which is a rather rude way for a visiting team to fail to participate in a numerical theme. Saffron won 52–0, and the argument about how it would respond to losing at Mossdeep lasted approximately as long as it took the Psi Corps to turn its first possession into a touchdown.

Trent Scarboro's team is 8–2. The Skyhawks are 3–7. Saffron gained 518 yards, made twenty-seven first downs and never punted. Fortree gained 146 yards, made six first downs and punted six times. There are blowouts with a strange turnover story attached to them, where a few disastrous bounces make the score look detached from the ordinary plays. This one spent most of the afternoon explaining itself in the ordinary plays.

Skattebo ran twenty-five times for 156 yards and five touchdowns. Archam Manning completed twenty-five of thirty-three passes for 329 yards and two scores without an interception or a sack. Gorebyss caught nine passes for 119 yards, Gengar Pickens five for 103. If you were looking for the one Saffron player Fortree should have stopped, the difficulty was choosing where to begin and discovering that the next choice had already gained another first down.

body.speaker: Dam Skattebo
body.text: The guys up front kept doing the hard part. Getting five chances to finish like that is special, and I appreciate every one of them. Everybody kept the drives moving. I got to be the one with the ball at the end.
The long way to a very short contest

The first Saffron touchdown required nine plays and seventy-five yards. Skattebo finished it on a four-yard run right with 3:19 left in the first quarter. Vikavolt's extra point went in off the upright. That was about as close as the afternoon came to making the Psi Corps' scoring operation look awkward. Fortree's first possession lost two yards and ended with a punt after Medicham sacked Rabsca on third-and-five.

Saffron then went sixty-seven yards in eleven plays. Skattebo took the final two yards up the middle early in the second quarter, and the lead became 14–0. Fortree managed fifteen yards before punting again. The Psi Corps' next drive covered eighty-one yards in nine plays, Skattebo scoring from six yards out on another run through the middle. Three possessions, three touchdowns, three different stretches of field traversed without needing the defense to provide a short starting point.

That is the part I would circle before circling the final score. Saffron's first three touchdown drives began with seventy-five, sixty-seven and eighty-one yards to cover. The offense did not merely accept a few convenient scoring chances. It repeatedly moved down the field against a defense that could not make the possession stop. Fortree had come in off three straight victories, over Vermilion, Fuchsia and Cerulean. Whatever confidence those wins had built, it offered no substitute for a third-down stop here.

At 1:28 before halftime, Medicham dropped Rabsca for another six-yard loss on third-and-eight. Fortree punted, Saffron covered sixty yards in four plays, and Manning's deep-left throw to Pickens became a thirty-yard touchdown at 0:54. It was 28–0 after the extra point. The Psi Corps had used Skattebo to finish the first three drives and now gave Fortree a reminder that the field also extended behind the linebackers.

body.speaker: Archam Manning
body.text: We stayed with the possession in front of us. The score grew because we kept doing that. When the running game is working and the receivers are finding room, my job is to make the decision cleanly and give them a useful ball.

Fortree still had time to make the half worse. Furfrou intercepted Rabsca's deep-left pass with thirty-three seconds remaining and returned it five yards. Saffron turned that opportunity into Vikavolt's thirty-nine-yard field goal at 0:03. Twenty-four points in the second quarter had made it 31–0. This time there was a turnover to mention, but it arrived after the home offense had already built four touchdown possessions. The interception added to the imbalance; it did not create it.
Five sacks from one address

Medicham recorded all five Saffron sacks. The losses totaled thirty-two yards, and his defensive line also included sixteen pressures. The individual sacks came on third-and-five in the first quarter, third-and-eight in the second, third-and-six in the third, then first-and-ten and second-and-nine in the fourth. Three of the five arrived on third down. That is a direct way to turn a quarterback's chance to extend a drive into a punter's next assignment.

Fortree's running game supplied very little relief. Floatzel carried four times for one yard. Rabsca completed fifteen of twenty-nine passes for 145 yards, but the Skyhawks had no passing touchdowns and one interception. A team playing from far behind will naturally ask its quarterback for more. Fortree did not get the productive early possessions that might have allowed it to avoid that situation. The score and the rush made each subsequent series harder to organize.

Saffron did not need a mountain of takeaways to keep the shutout intact. Furfrou's interception was the only one, and Fortree lost no fumbles. The Psi Corps repeatedly defended the downs in front of it, forced punts and returned the ball to an offense that was already moving. The final third-down comparison was five of seven for Saffron and three of ten for Fortree. Those are very different ways to spend a football game.

The first second-half Saffron touchdown drive went ninety-three yards in ten plays. Skattebo ran left for the final five at 1:44 of the third quarter. Fortree's next series again ended in a punt, helped along by Medicham's seven-yard sack. Manning then found Mothel Irving short right for a five-yard touchdown on third-and-two early in the fourth. The Psi Corps had found room for another receiver in the end zone while its leading scorer waited for one more turn.

That turn came after an eight-play scoring drive and another Fortree punt had given way to Saffron's final touchdown march. The Psi Corps went fifty-seven yards in ten plays, and Skattebo ran up the middle for a one-yard score with 1:18 remaining. His five touchdown runs measured four, two, six, five and one yard. The longest was six. The offense had done the transportation; Skattebo handled the final delivery five separate times.

body.speaker: Trent Scarboro
body.text: We needed to keep completing drives. I was pleased with how many different players helped us get into position, and with the defense getting us the ball back. The next opponent won't care how many points we scored today.
The next test will not be this one

Fortree's last possession at least lasted. The Skyhawks went sixty-four yards in thirteen plays before turning the ball over on downs, and Manning ended the game with a kneel. The late progress did not produce points, but it also should not be retroactively reassigned to a different part of the game. Fortree's final yardage total includes work done after the competitive question had been settled. That is one reason the twenty-seven-to-six first-down gap may be the afternoon's cleanest description.

Manning spread his completions among six receivers. Gorebyss made nine catches on ten targets; Pickens had the thirty-yard touchdown and a forty-yard long gain in his five-catch day; Irving finished with six catches for fifty-three yards and a score. HeeDee Lamb added thirty-six receiving yards, and Dipplin eighteen. Saffron's rushers combined for 189 yards. Fortree could not contain the ground game without leaving itself a passing problem, and it never solved the passing problem either.

The win came with a cost. Emmitt Smoth is listed out two weeks after this game. Saffron also still has Ninetales and Verrick Brooks listed out one week each. Medicham's performance is even more useful in that context, although one spectacular afternoon does not make unavailable teammates unimportant. The Psi Corps will prepare for Cinnabar with the players who can actually take the field, not the ones a 52-point score might make everyone forget are missing.

Fortree lost Pawmot for six weeks. Rabsca and Banette received minor injury entries in the game report, but the longer absence belongs to the defensive end. Winona's team now visits Mauville. A three-game winning streak had suggested some repair; this result demonstrated how far the Skyhawks remain from controlling a game against a strong opponent. The next assignment starts with making a possession last and preventing the other offense from treating every drive as an appointment in the end zone.

Saffron's assignment is more demanding than a victory lap. Cinnabar is 7–3 and comes off a bye. The Psi Corps have allowed seventy points all season, but the trip to Mossdeep showed that a quality opponent can still make the decisive plays against them. This response establishes that Saffron could put the disappointment behind it for one week. It does not award any of the points needed on the road next week.

Still, Scarboro has every right to appreciate the completed work: seven touchdowns, a field goal, no punts, no giveaways, five sacks and a shutout. Skattebo can hand out all the credit he likes. Fortree spent the afternoon handing him the ball back within reach of another score. By the time he took the last yard, the answer was fifty-two.

art.alt: Dam Skattebo and five footballs celebrate a five-touchdown afternoon.

articles.title: Eighty-four yards of nowhere
articles.dek: Mt. Silver held Eterna to three first downs and zero third-down conversions. Tic Thorpe threw four touchdowns in a 38–0 win that sends the unbeaten Reds into their Blackthorn showdown.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Eterna gained eighty-four yards. Please sit with that number before somebody tries to sell you a sophisticated objection to Mt. Silver's place among the league's best. Eighty-four yards, three first downs, zero successful third downs in eight attempts. The Reds won 38–0, improved to 10–0, and invited the Thorns to spend most of the afternoon deciding which direction their punter should face.

Tic Thorpe threw four touchdown passes. Connor McLarren's offense gained 352 yards and did not surrender a sack or an interception. Those are excellent facts. I am beginning with the defense because Eterna arrived 6–3, carrying three straight wins over Olivine, Cianwood and Azalea, and left with the same number of points it had when the game began. The Thorns were a credible opponent. Mt. Silver made credibility very difficult to spot once the ball was snapped.

The Reds have now shut out Canalave and Eterna in consecutive games, winning those two by a combined 72–0. Across ten games, they have allowed sixty-eight points. That is 6.8 per game. If you insist on discussing only the most spectacular offense in the league, you can have that discussion. The uncomfortable truth is that somebody will eventually have to score against this defense to make the discussion matter.

body.speaker: Tic Thorpe
body.text: We kept getting another possession. The defense made that possible. I needed to use them.
Three and out became an itinerary

The first Eterna possession covered nine yards and ended in a punt. Mt. Silver answered with a punt of its own, which is a useful reminder that the Reds did not start the day by scoring every time they touched the ball. Then the Thorns lost a yard on their next possession and punted again. McLarren's offense had another chance before Gardenia's group had produced anything resembling a lasting foothold.

Mt. Silver's first touchdown drive went seventy-seven yards in ten plays. Thorpe found Tentacool short right for a five-yard score with 1:19 remaining in the opening quarter. Adam Venutieri converted the kick. Eterna's next possession gained five yards and ended in another punt. This was becoming a recurring exchange: the Thorns briefly borrowed the ball, the Reds got it back, and Thorpe was given enough opportunities to find the next scoring drive.

The next one covered fifty-eight yards in nine plays. Plusico Buress caught Thorpe's six-yard short-left touchdown with 4:03 left in the second quarter. Eterna gained two yards and punted. Mt. Silver then went fifty-nine yards in ten plays, finishing on fourth-and-five when Thorpe hit Nuzleaf short middle for exactly five yards and a touchdown. The decision required execution, and the offense supplied it. The score became 21–0 after the extra point.

Three touchdown drives of ten, nine and ten plays are a particular kind of discouragement. The opponent has time to make a stop. It sees third downs, short gains and chances to create a mistake. Then the possession keeps going. Thorpe did not need a sixty-yard touchdown to build this lead. He needed the Reds to complete the next useful snap often enough, and the defense kept providing the next possession when the offense had finished.

Eterna's final full series before halftime ended with Blayz Matthews sacking Tatsugiri for six yards on third-and-four. Another punt followed. The Thorns' last play of the half gained four yards, but there were no points to accompany it. The Reds went to the break with a three-touchdown lead and a defense that had spent the first half preventing even the modest progress required to sustain a drive.

body.speaker: Connor McLarren
body.text: We kept asking the defense to finish the series, and they did. Offensively, the long drives were important. You want to reward the stops with something more than another quick trip back onto the field.
A quarterback can appreciate this workplace

Thorpe completed twenty-three of forty passes for 252 yards. His four touchdown throws went to four different receivers: Tentacool, Buress, Nuzleaf and Tony Gyarzalez. He was not sacked and did not throw an interception. The offense also ran twenty-four times for exactly one hundred yards. There was enough variety to keep the ball moving and enough protection to let the quarterback keep deciding where it should go.

Gyarzalez led the receivers with six catches for seventy-four yards. Buress added sixty-eight on four catches, Scep Smith Jr. forty-six on four, and Doduo thirty-eight on three. The Reds were playing without Gregar Jenings, who remains listed out one week, and Josh Alakazam's season injury remains on the report. Those absences are real. So is an offense distributing four touchdown passes without asking an unavailable player to rescue it.

The third quarter began with a Mt. Silver punt, followed by Eterna's most productive drive to that point. It ended badly. Tatsugiri's deep-right pass was intercepted by Mach Singltery at 4:04, and the return gained thirteen yards. A small opening for the visitors became another possession for the Reds. Mt. Silver turned that into a six-play, fifty-nine-yard touchdown drive, finished by Thorpe's short-left throw to Gyarzalez for thirty-one yards.

At 28–0, Eterna still could not make third down useful. The game ended with the Thorns zero for eight in that category. Tatsugiri completed eight of nineteen passes for forty-one yards and the interception. Stantler carried eleven times for forty-one yards; Ambipom added two on one attempt. Those numbers account for the entire forty-three-yard rushing total. Even the best available way to move the ball was producing yards in quantities too small to reverse the game.

body.speaker: Tony Gyarzalez
body.text: We don't have to make every throw the biggest one. The shorter completions matter, too. If everybody keeps working, one of them can become a bigger play. Tic gave us those chances all day.

Gardenia's defense did interrupt the Reds. It forced four punts and recorded eight passes swatted. That deserves to be recorded precisely, because a shutout does not mean every player on the losing team spent every snap failing. The problem was that the Eterna offense could not turn those stops into sustained possession or points. The defense would get the ball back, and soon it was being asked to do the same job again.

Mt. Silver ran sixty-four plays to Eterna's thirty-two. That is not a poetic way of saying it controlled the game. It is the actual count, and it helps explain why the scoreboard kept growing even though the Reds had unproductive possessions of their own. A defense asked to play twice as many snaps is exposed to twice as many opportunities for something to go wrong. The Thorns did enough to interrupt the afternoon, never enough to redirect it.
Now bring on Blackthorn

The fourth-quarter touchdown drive was the longest by play count: twelve snaps, seventy-two yards and 3:45. Vibrava finished it with a three-yard run up the middle at 1:19. Raticate had gained fifty-two yards on eleven carries; Vibrava finished with forty-eight on thirteen and the score. The ground game had not produced a breakaway longer than eight yards between those two backs. It had still supplied one hundred yards and helped occupy possession after possession.

Eterna turned the ball over on downs on its next series. Venutieri then made a forty-four-yard field goal with twelve seconds left, completing his eight-point afternoon. The Thorns ended the game with thirteen yards over their last two plays. Add everything up and the total remains eighty-four. Mt. Silver finished with seventeen first downs to Eterna's three, one takeaway to none, and a second straight clean sheet.

The Reds lead Kanto–Johto's current seeding order. Blackthorn comes next at 8–2, fresh from a 21–20 defeat to Sunyshore in which Hatterene threw for 368 yards and three touchdowns. That is a much more forceful passing line than anything Eterna produced here. It is the right next test for a defense that has made consecutive opponents look stuck. I want to see the Dragons try it. I suspect McLarren does, too.

There is no need to pretend that a 10–0 record has already awarded Mt. Silver a postseason result. Seven regular-season games remain, and every future touchdown must still be earned or prevented. But there is equally little need to treat ten straight victories as an interesting clerical accident. This team has a reliable way of reducing an opponent's opportunities, then enough offense to use the opportunities that creates. That combination travels well into any serious discussion of the Indigo Bowl.

Eterna falls to 6–4 and returns home to meet Sunyshore. The Thorns are still sixth in the Hoenn–Sinnoh seeding order, and Gardenia's immediate problem is more concrete than the table: restoring an offense that could not convert a single third down. The current injury report contains no remaining absence for Eterna. The corrections must come from the group that is available, including a passing game that produced forty-one yards on nineteen attempts.

Thorpe can celebrate four touchdown throws. Gyarzalez can appreciate the thirty-one-yard score. Matthews and Singltery can point to the sack and interception that punctuated the defense's work. My favorite number is still the smallest useful one: three. That is how many first downs Eterna made in an entire game. Blackthorn, your turn.

art.alt: A crimson defensive wall illustrates Mt. Silver’s second consecutive shutout.

articles.title: Lavender finds its feet, then counts the cost
articles.dek: Diggersby scored on the ground and through the air as the Wails beat Veilstone 31–14 and returned to .500. Injuries to People Eater and Beedrill complicate the next step.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: Diggersby did not offer a grand explanation for Lavender's recovery. There had been a gap, he said, and he had gone through it. That description covered his thirty-one-yard touchdown run reasonably well. It did not quite cover what a 31–14 victory over Veilstone meant to a Wails team that had lost four straight and spent the previous week struggling to reach even one touchdown.

Lavender is back at 5–5. Diggersby ran for 101 yards and a score, caught two passes for twenty-seven yards and another touchdown, and helped give Travis Scarboro's offense the balance it had been missing in its latest result. Mr. Clanky completed twenty-three of thirty-four passes for 223 yards and two touchdowns, adding a rushing score. The Wails produced 367 yards, seventeen first downs and four touchdowns. A week after scoring seven at Pastoria, those were welcome changes.

I would like to leave the afternoon there, with the offense looking more like itself and the season still available to be improved. The injury report makes that impossible. People Eater is out six weeks and Beedrill one. They combined for nine catches here. Lavender won the game and lost availability in the same receiving group it needs to keep the offense moving. A good result can carry two messages without either one cancelling the other.

body.speaker: Diggersby
body.text: There was room, so I went. The guys made it pretty straightforward for me. I'm not going to make it sound more complicated just because it ended in a touchdown.
The first quarter offered a choice

The opening minutes did not suggest an entirely comfortable afternoon for Mr. Clanky. Octillery sacked him for six yards on second-and-five, and the Wails had to deal with pressure before their passing game had settled. Veilstone then gave Lavender the first major opportunity. Tatsugiri threw deep left on third-and-five at 3:45, Picasso intercepted and returned the ball fourteen yards. The Wails had the ball back and a chance to make their early difficulties temporary.

Octillery sacked Clanky again during the ensuing possession. Lavender still finished it. On fourth-and-four at 1:56, the quarterback ran left for four yards and a touchdown. Just a cactus converted the kick. There is something reassuring about an offense completing a drive after its quarterback has been knocked backward. The sack did not have to become the defining event. Clanky's fourth-down run made the definition seven points instead.

Veilstone's next interception arrived at 1:09 of the first quarter. Stunfisk took Tatsugiri's deep-left pass and returned it eighteen yards. Lavender again converted the turnover into a touchdown, this time on Clanky's short-left throw to Diggersby for twenty-five yards with two seconds left in the quarter. The extra point made it 14–0. Two takeaways had become two touchdowns, and the Wails had given themselves room to play the rest of the game with a lead.

Those were not turnovers that can be discussed separately from the offense's response. A defense can win the ball and still watch the next possession disappear without consequence. Lavender made the opportunities count. Picasso and Stunfisk supplied the interceptions; Clanky and Diggersby supplied the finishes. The names belong together in the account of the start. It was a shared repair to a team that had needed more from both sides of the ball.

body.speaker: Mr. Clanky
body.text: The defense gave us chances. We finished them. That helped.

At 4:10 of the second quarter, Diggersby ran left for thirty-one yards and another touchdown. Lavender led 21–0 after the conversion. His earlier receiving score had come on a short-left throw; the rushing score now gave him two different ways of reaching the same destination. He finished with fifteen carries, a 6.7-yard average and a long run equal to that touchdown. Nothing else in his rushing line had to be spectacular for the whole afternoon to be productive.
Useful work between the scores

Samurott led Lavender's receivers with sixty-seven yards on six catches. Beedrill caught seven passes for sixty, Diggersby two for twenty-seven and Luvdisc two for twenty-three. People Eater, Frosmoth and Carnivine each supplied additional completions. Clanky completed passes to seven different receivers. That distribution matters now because the injury report will change the available group, and the offense needs more than a single preferred answer to keep working.

Clanky was not mistake-free. Ampharos intercepted his deep-left pass with 1:49 left before halftime and returned it twenty-one yards. Veilstone turned the chance into Tatsugiri's five-yard short-middle touchdown to Azumarill at 0:43. The Fists went to the break down 21–7, having finally made something useful happen with a possession. The Wails had built a large enough lead to survive one error, but the error still supplied the opponent's first points.

Maylene's team found some defensive resistance throughout the afternoon. Octillery's two sacks and Sandslash's one brought Clanky down three times for seventeen yards. Lavender also missed two field goals, with Just a cactus finishing one of three. A 31-point total does not mean the offense completed every opportunity. The more encouraging point is that it created enough opportunities to absorb those failures and still win by seventeen.

Third down was a much better place for Lavender than for Veilstone. The Wails converted seven of twelve, the Fists four of thirteen. Lavender punted only twice; Veilstone punted six times. Those figures help explain the yardage gap without requiring every successful possession to appear in a highlight reel. Moving the chains a little more often keeps the offense on the field and gives its good players another chance to contribute.

The Wails' defense also held Tatsugiri to ten completions on twenty-eight attempts. He finished with 120 yards, two touchdowns and two interceptions. Veilstone ran twenty times for seventy-six yards, sixty of them from Vigoroth. That ground production gave the visitors some progress, but it could not erase the turnovers or consistently replace the completions they needed. Lavender swatted seven passes, and the game became a long search for the Fists' next sustainable drive.

body.speaker: Travis Scarboro
body.text: We gave ourselves a lead by finishing the opportunities the defense created. I liked the way we kept moving the ball after that. The injuries are difficult, and now we have to get the next group ready to do its part.
A quieter third, a necessary fourth

Neither team scored in the third quarter. The recorded sack of Tatsugiri at 3:02 came on third-and-one and cost seven yards, turning a manageable down into another interrupted possession. The defensive box score splits Lavender's one sack between Mauler Twin and Grimace Shake. That is a small accounting distinction, but an appropriate one on a day when the defense's most useful work often involved more than the player nearest the ball at the end.

Lavender's next touchdown arrived on the opening recorded snap of the fourth quarter. Clanky went deep right to Luvdisc for thirteen yards on second-and-six, and the conversion made it 28–7. Luvdisc caught both passes directed his way. His afternoon was smaller than Diggersby's, Samurott's or Beedrill's by volume, yet this completion supplied the score that made a comfortable lead much harder for Veilstone to challenge.

Just a cactus finally added a field goal from fifty-two yards with 1:18 remaining. The kick made it 31–7. Veilstone then put together a late drive, finishing with Tatsugiri's four-yard short-left touchdown to Ponyta on fourth-and-four at 0:06. The extra point created the final score. Ponyta finished with four catches for fifty-six yards, the largest receiving total on the visiting side. The late touchdown rewarded that last possession without changing who had controlled the afternoon.

The distinction matters because Lavender's defense had done enough well to deserve credit without receiving an imaginary shutout. The Fists scored twice, once after an interception and once in the closing seconds. They also finished with only nine first downs to the Wails' seventeen and 196 yards to 367. There is a clear improvement to discuss here. There is no need to decorate it by pretending the opponent never moved.
The relief has a next address

People Eater had caught two passes for sixteen yards and run once for twelve. Beedrill's seven catches came on eleven targets. Their injury timing is not established in the recorded report, and it would be unfair to build a dramatic turning-point scene around a time we do not have. The present consequence is clear enough: six weeks without People Eater and one without Beedrill will ask other receivers to take on more responsibility.

Lavender travels to Cianwood next with the seventh spot in Kanto–Johto's current playoff order. That is a position in the standings, not a secured place in the postseason. The Wails are level at .500, still carrying a season point differential of minus sixty-eight, and have seven regular-season games left. Scarboro has a useful result to build on, but neither the record nor the schedule allows him to treat this as a completed recovery.

Veilstone is 4–7, winless in six road games and headed to Snowpoint. The Fists have lost three straight. Maylene's immediate work includes protecting the ball early enough that the game does not have to be repaired from a three-touchdown deficit. Their two interceptions here arrived before the first quarter was over. By the time the offense supplied its first touchdown, Lavender had already scored three.

I am willing to let the Wails enjoy the difference from last week. Thirty-one points is a much more pleasant total to discuss than seven, and Diggersby's one hundred rushing yards gave the conversation an agreeable starting place. The injury news will follow them into the next preparation. So will a simpler memory: a run left, thirty-one yards, and a back who thought the opening was too useful to overexplain.

art.alt: Diggersby and Mr. Clanky share a cheerful Lavender sideline.
